page_title: Disk Read and Write Speed Test
page_content:
> Section: Server Operations / Windows Server Operations
> Applies to: Windows Server 2008 R2 or later, Windows 7 or later (32/64-bit)
> Tool: Parkdale 3.08 (free, portable, no installation required)

## 1. Overview
When a server runs slow queries, lags during video playback, or takes a long time to boot, the cause is often **insufficient disk throughput** rather than the application itself. CPU and memory exhaustion raise alarms, but a slow disk is usually silent — every indicator looks normal while the amount of data actually written to disk per second is far below what is needed.

A single Parkdale benchmark gives you the real read and write capability of the machine, which helps you determine:

- Whether the disk meets its rated performance (HDD, SATA SSD, NVMe, cloud volumes, and RAID arrays differ enormously)
- Whether the disk is aging, has bad sectors, or has lost its cache advantage
- Whether a cloud volume is being rate-limited (same specification from different vendors can differ by 3–5×)
- Whether replacing disks, expanding capacity, or moving to a RAID array actually brought improvement

## 2. Getting the Software

Parkdale is developed by the sz development (Germany) and is distributed free of charge from the official website. It is **portable** — extract and run, no installation.

**Official download (the only trustworthy source)**

- Product page: <https://www.the-sz.com/products/parkdale/>
- Windows direct link: <https://www.the-sz.com/common/get.php?product=parkdale>

**Attachment**: [Parkdale-3.08-official.zip](http://pug2.4000329988.com/fqa/server/index.php?s=/api/attachment/visitFile&sign=db9c0528aab07701e6077af195aa9400 "[Parkdale-3.08-official.zip") is attached to this article. It was downloaded unchanged from the official site above; extract it and run `Parkdale.exe` directly.

**Verification data** (check the package yourself to confirm it is genuine)

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Filename | Parkdale.zip |
| Version | 3.08 |
| Size | 849 KB (869,129 bytes) |
| SHA256 | `20ad93d321dd30672d482603b9a3eaa1e1b1317ee5cefaaa15f439fe320da45b` |
| Company | the sz development |

> ⚠️ **Important**: Many third-party "disk tool" download sites repackage Parkdale and may bundle adware or ship a modified executable. Obtain it only from the-sz.com or from the attachment on this page.
>
> To verify, open PowerShell on Windows and run
> `Get-FileHash Parkdale.zip -Algorithm SHA256`.
> If the result matches the value above, the package is the official release.
>
> You can also install it through a package manager, which pulls from the official source:
> `winget install --id the-sz.Parkdale -e`

![](http://pug2.4000329988.com/fqa/server/index.php?s=/api/attachment/visitFile&sign=6373e347d784e4b722657b39224089ad)
## 3. Operating Instructions

Place `Parkdale.exe` in any directory on the server (for example `D:\tools\`), **double-click to run**, then follow three steps:

1. Select the target disk in the left-hand list
2. Leave `File Size` at the default value of `1000` MB
3. Click **Start** and wait for the benchmark to finish (about 10–60 seconds depending on disk speed)

Four results are reported: sequential write speed, 4 KB random write, sequential read speed, and 4 KB random read.

> **Note**: The test writes a 1000 MB temporary file to the target volume and deletes it automatically when finished. Before testing the system volume, make sure at least 2 GB is free. On production servers, avoid running the benchmark during peak hours.

## 4. Reference Results

The following measurements were taken on different storage media and can serve as a baseline for judging whether a given machine's disk performance is normal.

### 4.1 Cloud Server SSD (Aliyun)

KVM virtualization platform, disk presented as a Red Hat VirtIO paravirtual device.
![](http://pug2.4000329988.com/fqa/server/index.php?s=/api/attachment/visitFile&sign=e34d32ca5e07a52de8a0abb339d59c78)

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| Sequential write | 106.1 MB/s |
| Sequential read | 106.3 MB/s |
| 4 KB random write | 7.9 MB/s, 2009.7 IOPS, 0.50 ms |
| 4 KB random read | 7.8 MB/s, 2002.5 IOPS, 0.50 ms |

> Cloud volume sequential speed is capped by the **bandwidth quota** of the instance, so it is not comparable to a local SSD running at 500 MB/s or more. These figures are normal for an entry-level cloud disk and do not indicate a fault.

### 4.2 Notebook SSD (Apple MacBook, BootCamp)
![](http://pug2.4000329988.com/fqa/server/index.php?s=/api/attachment/visitFile&sign=549549e3b7c2427085cba94671823aed)

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| Sequential write | 609.4 MB/s |
| Sequential read | 474.2 MB/s |
| 4 KB random write | 19.7 MB/s, 5051.2 IOPS, 0.20 ms |
| 4 KB random read | 18.5 MB/s, 4745.9 IOPS, 0.21 ms |

> Typical NVMe SSD performance. With over 5000 IOPS and 0.2 ms random access latency, this class of drive handles database workloads very well.

### 4.3 Server SSD Array (Dell PERC H730P)
![](http://pug2.4000329988.com/fqa/server/index.php?s=/api/attachment/visitFile&sign=f5d898af07c02b6c45bf4c584c1d6c00)

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| Sequential write | 2028.4 MB/s |
| Sequential read | 606.4 MB/s |
| 4 KB random write | 42.7 MB/s, 10925.0 IOPS, 0.09 ms |
| 4 KB random read | 42.5 MB/s, 10885.7 IOPS, 0.09 ms |

> An SSD array behind a RAID controller with write cache. Sequential write exceeds 2000 MB/s (the write cache is doing its job), IOPS are above 10,000, and latency is 0.09 ms — the ideal state for a database server.

### 4.4 Ordinary HDD (HGST HTS721010A9E630)
![](http://pug2.4000329988.com/fqa/server/index.php?s=/api/attachment/visitFile&sign=3bebf0ea745b7bde38cff4d7136d0867)

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| Sequential write | 65.2 MB/s |
| Sequential read | 110.1 MB/s |
| 4 KB random write | 554.7 KB/s, 138.7 IOPS, 7.21 ms |
| 4 KB random read | 1020.7 KB/s, 255.2 IOPS, 3.92 ms |

> A typical 5400/7200 RPM 2.5-inch hard drive. **Random access latency of 3–7 ms is 20–40× that of an SSD** — which is exactly why "the database is on a spinning disk and it is slow". Sequential throughput is adequate, but small-file and index lookups suffer badly.

### 4.5 Server SAS HDD (Dell R710, SEAGATE ST3600057SS)
![](http://pug2.4000329988.com/fqa/server/index.php?s=/api/attachment/visitFile&sign=effb2c6c9fc61f1c136abe635e4820ff)

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| Sequential write | 102.6 MB/s |
| Sequential read | 188.0 MB/s |
| 4 KB random write | 1102.6 KB/s, 275.6 IOPS, 3.63 ms |
| 4 KB random read | 1264.3 KB/s, 316.1 IOPS, 3.16 ms |

> A 15,000 RPM SAS drive. Both sequential and random performance clearly beat ordinary SATA HDDs, but it is still bound by mechanical seek time, so random latency remains above 3 ms.

## 5. Reading the Results

| Metric | Meaning | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Seq. Write Speed** | Sequential write | Relevant for large file copies and video recording |
| **Seq. Read Speed** | Sequential read | Relevant for large file reads and video playback |
| **Random QD32** | 4 KB random at queue depth 32 | Relevant for databases, VMs and small files |
| **IOPS** | I/O operations per second | Higher is better; SSD 5000+, HDD 100–300 |
| **ms** | Average access latency | Lower is better; SSD 0.1–0.3 ms, HDD 3–10 ms |

**How to judge**

- Sequential speed far below the rated value → check the interface (SATA II caps at 300 MB/s), cables, RAID mode, or cloud volume bandwidth quota
- Abnormally low random IOPS (HDD below 80) → possible bad sectors or severe fragmentation
- Results fluctuating more than 30% across repeated runs on the same disk → disk health is questionable; check SMART data
- Cloud server consistently below comparable machines → check for rate limiting or heavy host load

## 6. The Three Test Modes

Parkdale has three tabs at the top. **QuickAccess** is sufficient for daily use:

| Mode | How it works | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **QuickAccess** | Tests through the filesystem: sequential read/write plus 4 KB random with 32 threads; multiple drives can be tested in sequence with results written to a log | Routine checks and multi-drive comparison (**recommended**) |
| **FileAccess** | Reads and writes an ordinary file through the filesystem | When you need to simulate real file I/O |
| **BlockAccess** | Bypasses the filesystem and reads/writes disk sectors directly, with a transfer-rate graph | Diagnosing bad sectors and observing speed degradation over time |

A command-line build, `ParkdaleCmd.exe`, is available for unattended batch testing:

```
ParkdaleCmd.exe -d D:\ -s 1000 -b 1024 -l 1
```

Parameters: `-d` target drive, `-s` test file size in MB, `-b` block size in KB, `-l` write a log file (1 = yes, 0 = no).

## 7. Notes

- The test **actually writes** 1000 MB of data, which slightly consumes SSD endurance; there is no need to run it frequently (once a quarter, or when replacing a disk, is enough)
- Do not run a large test on a system volume with little free space — filling the volume will cause system problems
- Write cache on a RAID controller is only enabled when a BBU or supercapacitor is present; that is when 2000 MB/s-class write results appear
- Results inside a virtual machine are affected by host load and can vary noticeably between runs on the same VM
- These numbers measure **performance only**, not disk health; if you suspect a failing disk, combine them with SMART data (`smartctl -a`, CrystalDiskInfo)
